w:r.w:t: Full-Stack Social Media Web Application with

Pulse is a full-stack social media web application designed around a scalable, event-driven notification architecture. The platform enables users to create posts, follow each other, like and comment on content, and receive instant, real-time notifications powered by WebSockets and asynchronous background workers.

Unlike a basic CRUD application, Pulse is designed to production-level engineering standards: clean separation of concerns, asynchronous task queues, real-time communication layers, and a modular backend that can scale horizontally. This document covers the full product vision, system design, user flows, feature set, and deployment strategy.

Core Thesis: Every user interaction (like, comment, follow) triggers an event that flows through a queue, is processed by a background worker, and is delivered to the recipient in real-time — all without blocking the main API thread.

Pulse aims to be a production-grade demonstration of modern full-stack engineering. The platform balances simplicity of interface with depth of infrastructure, showing that real-world scalability patterns — event queues, WebSockets, background workers — can be built into an application from day one.

Pulse has three distinct user roles, each with different levels of access and capabilities within the system.
A guest is any visitor who has not logged in. Guests have read-only, limited access to public-facing pages. They cannot interact with any content.
An authenticated user has logged in and has full access to all social features of the platform. This is the primary user persona for Pulse.
Update profile information (bio, display name, avatar)
An administrator has elevated privileges accessed through the Django Admin Panel. Admins do not have a separate frontend interface — all admin actions occur via /admin.
View, edit, deactivate, delete any user account
View all notifications in the system
Pulse follows a layered, event-driven architecture. The system is composed of five distinct layers that communicate asynchronously where possible:
Event broker between API and workers
The notification system is the architectural centerpiece of Pulse. Every social interaction follows this exact pipeline:
The user performs an action — likes a post, comments, or follows someone. The frontend sends an authenticated HTTP POST request to the Django REST API.

The Django API receives the request. It: (a) validates the JWT token and identifies the acting user, (b) stores the interaction in the PostgreSQL database (like, comment, or follow row), and (c) immediately pushes a task event onto the Redis queue using Celery. The API returns a success response to the frontend without waiting for notification processing.

A Celery worker picks up the task event from the Redis queue. The worker: (a) checks if the recipient user has that notification type enabled in their preferences, (b) creates a Notification record in the database with type, message, sender, receiver, and is_read = False, (c) checks if the recipient is currently online via their WebSocket connection state, and (d) sends a WebSocket event to the Django Channels layer if the user is online.

Django Channels receives the WebSocket push event and routes it to the specific user's WebSocket connection group. The notification data (type, message, sender username, timestamp) is serialized and transmitted to the browser in real time.

The browser's WebSocket listener receives the notification payload. The notification bell count increments instantly. If the user is on the Notifications page, the new notification appears at the top of the list without requiring a page refresh.
OFFLINE PATH — Stored for Later Retrieval

If the recipient is offline (no active WebSocket), the notification still gets stored in the database by the Celery worker. When the user next logs in, the frontend fetches their unread notification count and full notification list via REST API on mount. Optionally, an email notification can be queued by a secondary Celery task.

Pulse uses PostgreSQL as its primary relational database. The schema is designed for normalized storage with foreign key relationships, and indexed fields for high-frequency query patterns.
likes.(user_id, post_id) — unique constraint + like status check
follows.(follower_id, following_id) — unique constraint + follow status

One User can have many Posts, Likes, Comments, and Follows. A Post belongs to one User and can have many Likes and Comments. A Notification connects a sender User to a recipient User, optionally referencing a Post or Comment. Each User has exactly one NotificationPreferences record (created on signup via signal).

All API endpoints are prefixed with /api/v1/. All requests require JWT Bearer token in the Authorization header except auth endpoints.

All notification processing is handled exclusively by Celery workers. No notification logic runs synchronously in API views. This ensures API response times are not impacted by notification overhead.

Broker: Redis (same instance as channel layer, separate DB index)
Result backend: Redis (for task state tracking)
Default queue: default — all notification tasks
Priority queue: high_priority — reserved for time-sensitive real-time events
Concurrency: 4 worker processes per Celery instance (configurable)
Task acknowledgment: on success (not on receive) — prevents data loss on worker crash
On max retry exceeded: task marked as failed, logged to Sentry (or error log)
Dead-letter pattern: failed tasks moved to failed_notifications queue for audit
Idempotency: tasks are safe to retry — duplicate notification prevention via DB constraints
Passwords: bcrypt with cost factor 12 (Django default)
